segments.text: It begins with understanding the OSHA hazard communication standard, because without communication,
you aren't able to foster awareness.
Everyone who might come in contact with the materials in question have to be aware of
their danger, their proper handling, and what to do when there is an emergency.
OSHA sets out some rules for communication standards, including that chemical manufacturers
and importers are required to evaluate the hazards of the chemicals that they produce
or import.
This includes preparing labels and safety data sheets that convey hazard information to downstream
customers.
Also, all employers with hazardous chemicals in their workplaces need labels and safety
data sheets for their exposed workers, and they need to offer adequate training so they
can handle these materials appropriately.
Employee training also has to include information on the hazards of their work area and any
measures they must take to protect themselves.
As with any communication, there are some basic terms to know.
Let's look at some essential terms as outlined by OSHA.
First is the action level.
This is set at an airborne level, typically one half of the PEL, or permissible exposure
limit, that's designated in OSHA's substance-specific standard.
That's 29 CFR 1910 subpart Z.
It's calculated as an eight-hour time-weighted average, which starts off certain required
activities like exposure monitoring and medical surveillance.
Then there's the ceiling limit.
That's the exposure limit a worker's exposure may never exceed.
Then you have sampling and analytical error.
This is a statistical estimate of the uncertainty that's associated when you're given exposure
measurement.
Then you have STEL, which is the short-term exposure limit.
That's the average exposure to a contaminant to which a worker might be exposed during
a short period of time, typically 15 to 30 minutes.
And finally, you have the TWA, which is the time-weighted average.
That's the average exposure to a contaminant over a given period of time, typically eight
hours.
Generally, we use two major terms across industries, combustible and flammable liquids.
OSHA outlines standards for what these are, but you've got to keep in mind the safety
standards might be different for construction zones.
Looking at combustible liquids, this is defined as any liquid having a flash point at or
above 100 degrees Fahrenheit.
For flammable liquids, it's defined as any liquid having a flash point below 100 degrees
Fahrenheit, excepting any mixture that has components with flash points of 100 degrees
Fahrenheit, or higher, the total of which make up 99% or more of the total volume of
the mixture.
Generally speaking, you might notice that flammable is used as a catch-all term which
comprises a wide range of risks.
